applicable_when: The kernel performs a GEMM (M=490, N=320, K=1152) with BLOCK_M=64, BLOCK_N=64, BLOCK_K=32 and 128 threads (4 warps). The B matrix has stride_bn=1152 (column-major), causing the BLOCK_K x BLOCK_N tile load to access B with a stride-1152 pattern that creates 12-way shared memory bank conflicts — 77.72% of all shared load wavefronts are wasted on conflicts. This directly causes 66.9% of all warp stall cycles (CPIStall/MIO). Additionally, 128 registers/thread x 128 threads = 16,384 registers/block limits occupancy to 4 blocks/SM (25% theoretical, only 6.25% achieved). The grid of 80 blocks covers only 0.15 waves across 132 SMs, leaving most SMs idle. TF32 was previously attempted and failed correctness (max_diff=0.13 >> atol=0.001 for K=1152). The fix is to: (1) reduce tile sizes to BLOCK_M=32, BLOCK_N=32, BLOCK_K=64 to cut register pressure and allow more blocks/SM, and (2) add num_stages=3 software pipelining to overlap memory loads with compute and hide MIO latency.

strategy_title: Doubling BLOCK_N/K Doubles Registers, Kills Occupancy
strategy_description: Increasing BLOCK_N and BLOCK_K from 32 to 64 in a Triton GEMM kernel nearly doubled register usage per thread (92 → 164) and more than doubled dynamic shared memory per block (24.6 KB → 65.5 KB). This caused Block Limit Registers and Block Limit Shared Mem to drop from 5 to 3 blocks per SM, reducing theoretical occupancy from 31.25% to 18.75%. Although warp cycles per issued instruction improved (8.03 → 5.16) and bank conflict ways decreased (18-way → 12-way), the total executed instruction count nearly doubled (7.27M → 13.54M) and elapsed cycles increased by 23%, resulting in a 22% regression. The bank conflict reduction was real but insufficient to offset the occupancy loss and instruction count increase caused by larger tiles.
slow_pseudocode:
BLOCK_M: tl.constexpr = 64
BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr = 32  # power-of-2, causes 18-way bank conflicts
BLOCK_K: tl.constexpr = 32  # power-of-2, causes bank conflicts
# grid = (80, 1, 1) fixed
# registers_per_thread = 92, smem = 24.6 KB/block
# theoretical_occupancy = 31.25%, block_limit_regs = 5
fast_pseudocode:
BLOCK_M: tl.constexpr = 64
BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr = 64  # doubled to break bank conflicts
BLOCK_K: tl.constexpr = 64  # doubled to break bank conflicts
# grid = (80, 1, 1) fixed (unchanged)
# registers_per_thread = 164, smem = 65.5 KB/block
# theoretical_occupancy = 18.75%, block_limit_regs = 3
# RESULT: 22% slower despite fewer bank conflicts
applicable_when: Never — this specific change (doubling both BLOCK_N and BLOCK_K simultaneously in a register-heavy Triton kernel) causes register and shared memory pressure to dominate, reducing occupancy and increasing total instruction count more than the bank conflict reduction saves.
do_not_apply_when: When the kernel already has high register usage (≥90 registers/thread) and shared memory usage near SM limits. Doubling tile dimensions in both N and K simultaneously will double register pressure and quadruple shared memory usage, collapsing occupancy from the register and shared memory block limits. The bank conflict reduction (18-way → 12-way) is real but insufficient to compensate when instruction count nearly doubles and occupancy drops by ~40% of theoretical.
framework_notes: In Triton, increasing BLOCK_N and BLOCK_K as constexprs directly increases register pressure because the compiler must allocate registers for the larger accumulator tile (BLOCK_M × BLOCK_N) and input tiles. On H200 with 92 registers/thread baseline, going to 164 registers/thread cuts Block Limit Registers from 5 to 3 blocks/SM. The grid was not updated to reflect the larger tiles, so the same 80 blocks ran with more work per block but fewer concurrent blocks per SM.
